caption:
What was the Great Moon Hoax of 1835?

Starting 25 August 1835, The Sun in New York ran six articles announcing life and civilisation on the Moon — bison, single-horned goats, mini zebras, unicorns, bipedal tail-less beavers, and winged humanoids called Vespertilio-homo, man-bats, who built temples.

The discoveries were credited to Sir John Herschel and his travelling companion Dr Andrew Grant. Herschel was real. Grant was invented. The telescope was said to have a lens 24 feet across weighing 7 tons, carried from New England to South Africa. The series ended when the Sun turned that lens into a burning glass and set the observatory on fire.

On 16 September 1835 The Sun admitted the articles were fabricated. It never printed a retraction. Richard Adams Locke, a Sun reporter, publicly admitted writing them in 1840.

Still open: rumours persisted that other men helped, though there is no good evidence for anyone but Locke. Herschel was amused at first, then annoyed at having to answer people who thought it was serious. And the claim that the hoax permanently lifted The Sun's circulation has certainly been exaggerated in popular accounts.

Images: man-bat portrait from an 1836 Naples edition, courtesy of the New York Public Library; Benjamin Henry Day's 1835 lithograph of lunar animals; Nouvelles découvertes dans la Lune by Thierry Frères; the frontispiece of the Welsh Hanes y Lleuad; the 1859 New York reprint title page; and Gaetano Dura's 1836 Naples lithograph of a coach returning from the Moon. All public domain.
